LeCat: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data

Jimin Mun Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Email: jmun@andrew.cmu.edu    Maarten Sap ††thanks: Equal advising contribution. Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Yanai Elazar11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Bar-Ilan University
Abstract

Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM’s Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of “knowledge expression”. We first assess open-source pretrained models using 199 curated category-feature pairs and analyze their training data. Our findings suggest that strengthening context and category-feature co-occurrence likelihood (PMI) improve learning for larger models and verbatim rule-like statements diminish flexible category learning. To systematically isolate these effects, we then train a 68M model from scratch with precise control over the categorical information each sees in their training data, confirming that verbatim repetition reduces flexible learning but mixture of diverse knowledge expressions lead to more robust category learning. Together, our findings highlight that while contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models, how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining greatly impacts models’ acquisition of robust category knowledge.

1 Introduction

Category learning is fundamental to human intelligence (Murphy and Ross, 1994; Tenenbaum et al., 2006), enabling generalization from sparse samples (e.g., airplanes are fast) to large sets of unseen examples (e.g., red airplanes are fast, blue airplanes are fast). This capacity has been extensively studied in cognitive science and psychology (Banse et al., 2010; Markman and Ross, 2003; Rhodes et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2024), as well as in classical machine learning and computer vision (Jia et al., 2013; Lake et al., 2015). Unlike factual knowledge, which is typically isolated (e.g., the Louvre opened on August 10, 1793), category membership licenses broader inference: the Louvre is a museum, so it likely shares characteristics with other museums (Bloom et al., 1964; Krathwohl, 2002; Murphy and Ross, 2010). Yet this same inferential power can be harmful when applied inaccurately, as with social stereotypes (Beukeboom and Burgers, 2019; Sherman et al., 1998). Thus, for robust generalization, learners must also acquire exceptions and counter-stereotypes, and flexibly incorporate context.

In this work, we empirically investigate how language models learn to generalize and apply category knowledge under various contexts, focusing specifically on how pretraining data shapes model behavior. While prior work has established that language models acquire factual or world knowledge from pretraining data (Eldan and Li, 2023; Hoffmann et al., 2022) which has prompted extensive research on data curation (Longpre et al., 2024; Parmar et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025, e.g., ) and knowledge injection (Chang et al., 2024a; Lv et al., 2025, e.g., ), how LMs acquire and use category knowledge from data is poorly understood. Clarifying how LLMs robustly acquire category knowledge would inform efforts to reduce harmful associations such as stereotypes and biases (Bai et al., 2025), and promote more flexible, creative category representations that yield diverse outputs (Sassenberg et al., 2022; Kenett, 2025).

We develop LeCat, a framework to analyze the Learning of Category knowledge and usage in LLM outputs and its training data. Focusing on LLM outputs, we develop log-probability measure, validated with LLM-as-a-judge, for category knowledge memorization (i.e., generation of category knowledge in its basic form), generalization (i.e., extension to invariant contexts), and contextual flexibility (i.e., behavioral differences based on context). For examining how training data informs LLM outputs, LeCat draws from cognitive science (Markman and Ross, 2003) to measure the prevalence of five types of category knowledge expressions in data, including verbatim repetition of category-feature associations (e.g., “The airplanes are fast”), exceptions (e.g., “This airplane is not fast”), weakening contexts (e.g., “The airplanes with broken engines are not fast”), and more.

We first apply LeCat to open-data models of several sizes, Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023) and OLMo 3 (Olmo et al., 2025). At every scale, contextual flexibility remains difficult: models struggle to adjust which features they produce in context, especially when the context weakens or contradicts (i.e., is erroneous about) the category-feature association. In the pretraining data, the factors that support category learning shift with scale. Strengthening contexts and category-feature co-occurrence (measured by PMI) become more beneficial as models grow, with PMI correlating positively with learning only in larger models. Verbatim statements of category-feature associations, by contrast, hurt flexible knowledge use at every scale, possibly through memorization. Since pretraining data are heterogeneous, however, these findings remain correlational.

To test these trends causally and isolate individual expression types and paradigms such as curriculum ordering, we create a fully controlled pretraining corpus by adapting the TinyStories dataset (Eldan and Li, 2023) by injecting two fictional category-feature relations, valins–poor and pezzdens–fast. We train a 68M parameter model from scratch on each expression type alone, a random mixture of all types, and a curriculum-ordered mixture. The results confirm the open-model finding that flexible category knowledge is difficult to learn but a diverse mixture improves while verbatim repetition reduces flexible category learning.

Together, these findings show that pretraining data composition, not just exposure frequency, shapes category learning, that the effective composition shifts with model scale, and that contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models. Our work thus points to practical implications for stereotypes and factual learning in LLMs.

2 Background & Related Work

Category learning is fundamental to human cognition, enabling classification, generalization, and inference (Tenenbaum et al., 2006; Murphy and Ross, 2010; Barsalou, 2012). Humans acquire categories through diverse mechanisms—from explicit rules to implicit similarity detection (Minda et al., 2024; Murphy, 2004)—and readily accommodate exceptions to typical category structure (Heffernan et al., 2021). Crucially, human category representations are context-dependent: many categorical concepts are multi-dimensional and distributed across brain regions, allowing certain features to be more activated depending on context (Yee et al., 2012; Yee and Thompson-Schill, 2016). This flexibility supports accurate generalization, reduces stereotyping (Sassenberg et al., 2022), and facilitates creative reasoning (Kenett, 2025).

Prior work on LLM knowledge learning during pretraining has examined memorization (Ghosh et al., 2025), statistical rule-learning (Nguyen, 2024), and factual knowledge learning (Chang et al., 2024a; Sun et al., 2025; Nadkarni et al., 2026). Furthermore, works in LLM concept learning has explored concept associations (Im et al., 2026) and property inheritance between categorical classes (Misra et al., 2023). However, how LLMs acquire category knowledge and learn to generalize it robustly and flexibly remain underexplored. Inspired by the key components of human category learning, we investigate how memorization, generalization (i.e., application of category knowledge to unseen members under irrelevant contexts), and contextual flexibility (i.e., application of category knowledge that reflects the context) emerge in language models as a function of pretraining data. Extended discussion of prior works in human category learning and LLM knowledge learning during pretraining is in Appendix A.

3 LeCat: LLM Category Learning Analysis Framework

We introduce LLM evaluation and data analysis framework for learning categories (LeCat), building on work in cognitive science. First, we create an output evaluation framework using completion probes based on completion of target feature given category and varying contextual cues (§3.1). We then craft five types of category knowledge expressions to analyze and create synthetic data (§3.2).

3.1 LeCat-Output: LLM Evaluation

To evaluate category learning in LLM outputs, LeCat probes along three behavioral dimensions grounded in human category learning research (Murphy and Ross, 2010; Markman and Ross, 2003; Truman and Kutas, 2024): memorization of category-feature associations, generalization to unseen instantiations, and contextual flexibility in applying associations appropriately. We operationalize each dimension using completion-based probability probing, validated with an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation of output generations.

3.1.1 Target–Max Log-Probability Gap

We quantify category knowledge as the strength of association between a category cc (e.g., airplanes) and a feature ff (e.g., fast), operationalized as P⁡(f∣c)P(f\mid c) following prior work in semantic cognition (Markman and Ross, 2003). For different behaviors such as memorization, generalization, and contextual flexibility, we build contextual prefix as shown in Table 1. To measure category and feature association at each training step, we define a log-probability gap metric, measuring a gap between most probable completion token and target token. Let pθti(⋅∣x)p_{\theta_{t_{i}}}(\cdot\mid x) denote the model’s next-token distribution at step tit_{i} given input xx, and let ymax=arg⁡maxy​pθti​(y∣x)y_{\max}=\arg\max_{y}\,p_{\theta_{t_{i}}}(y\mid x) be the most probable next token. For a target token ytargety_{\text{target}}, we define:

G⁡(x,ytarget)=log⁡pθti​(ytarget∣x)−log⁡pθti​(ymax∣x).\begin{split}G(x,y_{\text{target}})={}&\log p_{\theta_{t_{i}}}(y_{\text{target}}\mid x)\\ &-\log p_{\theta_{t_{i}}}(y_{\max}\mid x).\end{split}

Higher values of GG (closer to 0) indicate greater model confidence in the target feature relative to competing predictions. We instantiate GG across three evaluation dimensions below. When target feature is not single token, we average across the token log probabilities.

Memorization captures the strength of the basic category-feature rule: whether the model produces “Airplanes are fast” even when this exact string was absent or rare in training (Ghosh et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024), reflecting feature production norms given a category (McRae et al., 2005). Given a base probe xx (e.g., “Airplanes are”), we set ytargety_{\text{target}} to the associated feature token (e.g., “fast”). A model that has acquired the association yields G⁡(x,ytarget)→0G(x,y_{\text{target}})\rightarrow 0 as training progresses. We denote this as GbaseG_{\text{base}}.

Generalization measures whether category knowledge transfers to unseen instances while remaining robust to over-generalization. For generalization to occur, models should be able apply knowledge to context changes that are invariant presence of a feature (e.g., “red airplanes are”), while in turn lowering its confidence when context contradicts it (e.g., “slow airplanes are”). Formally, for invariant contexts xinv=(c,ctxtinv)x_{\text{inv}}=(c,\texttt{ctxt}_{\text{inv}}), the model should preserve confidence in ytargety_{\text{target}}, yielding Gbase≳G⁡(xinv,ytarget)G_{\text{base}}\gtrsim G(x_{\text{inv}},y_{\text{target}}). For erroneous contexts xerr=(c,ctxterr)x_{\text{err}}=(c,\texttt{ctxt}_{\text{err}}), the model should assign lower confidence, yielding G⁡(xinv,ytarget)>G⁡(xerr,ytarget)G(x_{\text{inv}},y_{\text{target}})>G(x_{\text{err}},y_{\text{target}}). Together, correct generalization satisfies Gbase≳Ginv>GerrG_{\text{base}}\gtrsim G_{\text{inv}}>G_{\text{err}}.

Contextual Flexibility measures whether the model appropriately modulates feature confidence based on relevant contextual cues. Some contexts strengthen the association (e.g., “an airplane with a new engine”) while others weaken it (e.g., “an airplane with an old engine”). We denote these as GweakG_{\text{weak}} and GstrG_{\text{str}}.

For a model that has learned category knowledge flexibly, we expect the correct ordering of the probe-based metric to be

Gstr>Gbase≳Ginv>Gweak>Gerr.G_{\text{str}}>G_{\text{base}}\gtrsim G_{\text{inv}}>G_{\text{weak}}>G_{\text{err}}.

We test models’ alignment with this ordering through pass rate of pairwise ordering, e.g., whether the model passes the Gstr>GbaseG_{\text{str}}>G_{\text{base}} order.

3.1.2 LLM-as-a-Judge Validation

To test whether these log-probability results hold for actual model outputs, we use Qwen3.8-27B11 1 Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 as an LLM judge (Chang et al., 2024b) to evaluate free-form generations. For each generation, the judge annotates (1) whether the feature can be inferred and (2) the strength of the inference. To elicit the features, we use the respect prefixes from Sheng et al. (2019), which convert each probe into a template such as “XYZ are known for being” (e.g., “Red airplanes are known for being”; see Table 5 in Appendix C.1). Across the open-source models (Pythia and Olmo3), both judge annotations correlate positively and significantly with our measure (Spearman ρ=0.88\rho=0.88 for feature inference and ρ=0.87\rho=0.87 for inference strength, both p<.01p<.01; see Appendix B.1 for full results), indicating that our probability-based measure is a valid and computationally efficient proxy for category learning.

3.2 LeCat-Data: Pretraining Data Analysis and Generation Framework

Focusing on how training data shapes category knowledge, LeCat examines how different expressions of category knowledge in data lead to learning. Drawing on prior work in cognitive science (Markman and Ross, 2003), we consider four common types of expressions: verbatim repetition, instantiation, exceptions, and context dependence. We illustrate each type with real excerpts from The Pile (Gao et al., 2020). Formal definitions are given in Appendix B.2.

Verbatim Repetition (DrepetitionD_{\text{repetition}}). We begin with the simplest learning signal: explicit category–feature statements without variation, contrast, or context. Repeating knowledge in this way, especially in generic form, transmits essentialist beliefs and represents a top-down approach to learning concepts (Rhodes et al., 2012; Sloutsky and Deng, 2019; Yu et al., 2025). We operationalize this signal, for both detection and generation, as texts that state the generic claim without qualification, additional attributes, or context. For example, the following pretraining excerpt establishes the generic claim directly: “…3. Skyscraper – A skyscraper is a tall, continuously habitable building having multiple floors…” (skyscraper, tall).

Examples and Instantiations (DinstantiationD_{\text{instantiation}}). Category learning often arises from comparing multiple members of the same category and identifying their shared structure (Markman and Ross, 2003). This corresponds to a bottom-up approach to category learning (Sloutsky and Deng, 2019), and it tests whether a model can abstract the generic property from exemplars. Here the feature is expressed through an individual member described with additional attributes that do not bear on the feature, as in: “…Calm, collected and outwardly empathetic, she is all one would expect from a woman…” (woman, empathetic).

Learning Exceptions (DexceptionsD_{\text{exceptions}}). Humans also learn to accommodate exceptions, which are category members that violate expectations (Savic and Sloutsky, 2019). Accommodating them is essential for accuracy and supports flexible, non-stereotypical reasoning (Heffernan et al., 2021; Banse et al., 2010; Gocłowska et al., 2013). However, exceptions are harder to learn accurately (Heffernan et al., 2021), and their effects on category knowledge vary. They can have no effect, backfire and reinforce the rule (Kunda and Oleson, 1997), or discredit the rule (Simmons and Gelman, 2025). We therefore include exception expressions to study how LLMs learn exceptions and how exceptions affect category learning. These are texts in which a category member lacks the typical feature with no explanatory context, as in: “…I said that I hated to shoot such a small moose on opening day…” (moose, large).

Context-Dependent Associations (Ddep. strengthenD_{\text{dep. strengthen}}, Ddep. weakenD_{\text{dep. weaken}}). Many category–feature associations depend on context (Yee and Thompson-Schill, 2016; Yee et al., 2012). For instance, the association “airplanes are fast” may weaken with an old engine or in heavy rain. Such flexibility is crucial for applying category knowledge accurately (Truman and Kutas, 2024) and for reasoning beyond stereotypes (Banse et al., 2010). We distinguish contexts that strengthen the association (Ddep. strengthenD_{\text{dep. strengthen}}), where the feature holds and the context reinforces it, from contexts that weaken it (Ddep. weakenD_{\text{dep. weaken}}), where the feature is absent and the context accounts for its absence. The following excerpt adds a strengthening condition: “…Every day the cooks got four loads of oak charcoal from Nicolosi to keep the ovens always hot…” (oven, hot). In contrast, this excerpt adds a weakening condition: “…There were two knives in the kitchen, both blunt and rusted…” (knife, sharp). Ddep. weakenD_{\text{dep. weaken}} and DexceptionsD_{\text{exceptions}} both describe a member lacking the feature. They differ only in whether a context accounts for the missing feature. This contrast lets us test whether explicitly stated contexts lead to flexible category knowledge, and how they affect other objectives such as memorization and generalization.

Using the framework.

We use these operationalizations for both data analysis and synthetic data generation. For pretraining data analysis, we use an LLM classifier to characterize the distribution of each expression type in the data (§4). For full control in pretraining experiments, we use the expression types to generate synthetic training data (§5). Furthermore, we consider two orderings to mix different expressions during training: randomly shuffled expressions (DallD_{\text{all}}) and a curriculum from easy to hard (DcurriculumD_{\text{curriculum}} – repetition, instantiation, exceptions, then dependent contexts), motivated by the success of curriculum learning for accurate category learning in humans (Heffernan et al., 2021).

4 Open Model Analysis

Our first investigation examines how existing LLMs pretrained on large heterogeneous text corpora exhibit category learning. We analyze two families of models: Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023) and Olmo 3-Base (Olmo et al., 2025), as they are some of the few open-data LLMs with publicly available base models with varying sizes, checkpoints, and data. We run our analysis on the 10 available sizes of Pythia models (14m to 12b) and 2 sizes of Olmo 3 models (7b and 32b). We also analyze their training data, The Pile (Gao et al., 2020) and Dolma 3 (Olmo et al., 2025).22 2 dolma3_mix-6T-1025-7B

4.1 Setup

Data Analysis.

We analyze publicly available training data using both mention-based co-occurrence through PMI analysis, and LLM classifier for expression types with 4000 excerpts per category-feature pair with both category-feature co-occurrence set (2000) and category-only set (2000) sampled from the data. We verify the classifier performance with human validation (83% agreement). See Appendix B.3 for prompts and detailed human verification results.

Category and Feature Selection.

We use n=199n=199 category–feature pairs: 100 human-generated and 99 model-generated pairs, which lets us comprehensively investigate category-feature pairs, ones prevalent in human-generation and ones actually prevalent in model-generation. For the human-generated pairs, we selected object category–feature pairs from McRae et al. (2005) (n=50n=50), nationality-based stereotypes from the SeeGULL dataset (Jha et al., 2023) (n=34n=34), and gender-based stereotypes from GEST (Pikuliak et al., 2024) (n=16n=16). Examples include (lemons, yellow), (Japanese, hardworking), and (men, childish). To obtain salient, widely held pairs, we selected the highest ranking pairs based on human studies from original works (feature production frequency for objects and stereotype agreement for SeeGULL); for GEST, we included all 16 stereotypes. For the model-generated pairs, we collected highest-ranking features from the models’ final checkpoints using the generation probes in §3.1.2 with one dropped pair due to too few valid features. See Appendix D.1 for further details on the generated feature selection.

Probe Generation.

For each category-feature pair, we generate invariant, weakening, and strengthening contexts using GPT-5.5. All probes were human verified and edited for fluency. We generate five contexts for each probe variations and take the mean probability across the five probes when reporting the results. Additionally, for erroneous contexts, we used antonyms of the features for construction. The details of probe generation and examples are in Appendix C.1.

4.2 Results

Category Learning Results.

Figure 1 shows pass rates of four ordering pairs. The base–invariant pair improves steadily with scale: the pass rate rises from 71.4% for Pythia-14M to 95.5% for Pythia-2.8B and 6.9B. In contrast, the strengthening pair degrades with scale: the pass rate falls from 81.9% for Pythia-14M to near chance for the largest models (51.3% for Pythia-6.9B, 49.7% for OLMo-3-32B). Larger models thus increasingly assign the bare generic a higher likelihood than its instantiated variants, while strengthening contexts no longer raise the feature above the generic. We hypothesize that this is due to the effect of larger models more strongly memorizing the base category knowledge rather than becoming context sensitive. Two order pairs remain difficult at every scale. Models rarely rank weakening contexts above erroneous (pass rates of 10.1–24.1%), and the weakening–invariant edge stays near chance (44.7–58.3%). Thus, our results demonstrate that correct generalization and contextual flexibility is difficult for models, especially in larger models for distinguishing strengthening contexts.

Pretraining Data and Category Learning.

We correlate the mean pass rate over each order pair with statistics computed over the corresponding pretraining corpus (the Pile for Pythia and Dolma 3 for OLMo-3; Figure 2). These include document-level PMI between the category and feature, the percentage of co-occurring excerpts that the LLM classifier assigns to each expression type (§3.2), and the evenness (i.e., diversity) of expression types. We report Pearson rr, and we consider a correlation significant when its Spearman correlation survives a two-sided t-test with FDR correction using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (p<0.05p<0.05).

Overall, we observe that the correlations are weak with only two model-factor pairs significant after FDR correction. We observe varying correlation strength with model size with PMI. For Pythia models up to 410M parameters, PMI is uncorrelated with pass rate (−0.05≤r≤0.01-0.05\leq r\leq 0.01). From Pythia-1B onward it is consistently positive (r=0.07r=0.07–0.140.14), and it is significant for Pythia-12B (r=0.13r=0.13). OLMo-3 follows the same direction but neither model is significant: PMI is weakly negative for the 7B model (r=−0.08r=-0.08) and positive for the 32B model (r=0.09r=0.09).

Among expression types, the percentage of Ddep. strengthenD_{\text{dep. strengthen}} excerpts has the largest positive correlations. These peak at Pythia-410M (r=0.21r=0.21) and Pythia-12B (r=0.20r=0.20) and are strongest in significance for OLMo-3-32B (r=0.16r=0.16), where it is the only expression type that reaches significance. The percentage of DexceptionD_{\text{exception}} excerpts is negatively correlated with pass rate at every Pythia scale (r=−0.04r=-0.04 to −0.18-0.18, strongest for Pythia-1.4B and 12B), though none of these correlations is significant after correction, and it is near zero for OLMo-3 (r=−0.02r=-0.02 and −0.05-0.05). The percentage of DrepetitionD_{\text{repetition}} excerpts is also negative throughout (r=−0.04r=-0.04 to −0.14-0.14 for Pythia; −0.13-0.13 and −0.11-0.11 for OLMo-3). DinstantiationD_{\text{instantiation}} and expression-type evenness show no consistent trend. Overall, larger models appear to rely more on association strength and on explicitly strengthening contexts to learn flexible category knowledge, while pairs with more exceptions or plain repetitions in the data tend to be learned less well. Most of these trends, however, do not reach significance individually.

Category–Feature Pair Examples.

Figure 3 lists category–feature pairs that had the highest and lowest average score and their data distribution (PMI and expression types from each model’s pre-training corpus). To exclude pairs that reach the extremes by noise, a pair is eligible only if at least 75% of the pooled models rank it in their top (or bottom) 20 of 199 pairs. The clearest pattern appears among low-scoring object pairs: (blueberries, rich in antioxidants) and (hamsters, nocturnal) are dominated by DrepetitionD_{\mathrm{repetition}} (67% and 40% of excerpts, against medians of 0.7% and 1.2% over all pairs) and have high PMI (8.2 and 4.0, against medians of 3.2 and 1.9). These results hint at the possible effect of memorization due to repetitive or verbatim statements of the base association without much contextual variation.

In contrast, OLMo-3’s three highest-scoring pairs are all object pairs, such as (scissors, dangerous) and (sledgehammers, dangerous), and have a large share of Ddep.strengthenD_{\mathrm{dep.\,strengthen}} (19–32% of excerpts, against a median of 6%): the corpus ties the feature to the specific contexts in which it applies. The pair (Japanese, hardworking) is among the three lowest-scoring pairs for both model families, despite their different models and corpora. However, we note that their distribution of expressions are highly similar, emphasizing the role of data composition and stereotype expressions in category knowledge acquisition during pretraining beyond model families.

5 Controlled Pretraining

While our open-model experiments shed light onto models’ weak contextual flexibility and suggested data dependence, the findings could be confounded by the extremely heterogeneous types of documents contained in their training data. To address these confounds, we conduct controlled experiments where we train an LM from scratch on synthetic data with carefully controlled knowledge injections.

5.1 Setup

Category Injection and Training. We construct two fictional category-feature pairs: valins–poor, pezzdens–fast that mimic societal category and an object category. Each category knowledge expression data is generated using GPT-4o mini and validated with GPT-5-mini (Appendix E.1). Category data is injected at every 100 samples during training. Datasets consist of 2.1M samples total using TinyStories (Eldan and Li, 2023) as its base. We train for 4 epochs for all data variations. We train a randomly initialized GPT-2 model (68M).33 3 Due to computational budget limitations, we use relatively smaller model that nevertheless have been shown to have the ability to learn from limited data (Eldan and Li, 2023). Full training details are in Appendix E.3.

Evaluation Probes and Generation Prompts. We manually create three probes each for testing memorization and generalization, and six probes each for contextual sensitivity across two categories as shown in Table 1. Furthermore, to validate generation quality, we use four open-ended generation prompts for each category (e.g., “The valins are” and “The pezzdens are”). We score grammar, creativity, and consistency (SgrammarS_{\text{grammar}}, ScreativityS_{\text{creativity}}, SconsistencyS_{\text{consistency}}; integers 1–10) following Eldan and Li (2023). See Appendix C.3 for a full list of probes and prompts and Appendix E.4 for results.

5.2 Results

Table 2 reports pass rates for the controlled pretraining experiments, which isolate the effect of each data type. Training on the full mixture DallD_{\text{all}} gives the highest overall pass rate (0.51). DcurriculumD_{\text{curriculum}} and DdependentD_{\text{dependent}} follow closely and perform similarly to each other (0.49 each; differences from DallD_{\text{all}} of −0.016-0.016, 95% CI [−0.040,+0.017][-0.040,+0.017], and −0.020-0.020, [−0.035,−0.002][-0.035,-0.002]). Every single-type subset falls clearly below the mixture: DrepetitionD_{\text{repetition}} (−0.039-0.039, [−0.060,−0.012][-0.060,-0.012]), DinstantiationD_{\text{instantiation}} (−0.060-0.060, [−0.078,−0.033][-0.078,-0.033]), and DexceptionD_{\text{exception}} (−0.104-0.104, [−0.130,−0.081][-0.130,-0.081]).

The per-constraint pass rates show that each data type shapes a different part of the ordering, and no single type satisfies all of it. As in the open-source analysis, data that repeats the category–feature association without adding context does not support flexible category learning. DrepetitionD_{\text{repetition}} best preserves the default association (Base ≥\geq Irr.: 0.90), but strengthening contexts almost never raise the feature’s probability above the base sentence (Str. >> Base: 0.03). DdependentD_{\text{dependent}} shows the opposite pattern: it gives the strongest contextual strengthening (0.62), consistent with the positive correlation of Ddep. strengthenD_{\text{dep. strengthen}} excerpts in the open-source models, but it weakens the default association (0.35). DexceptionD_{\text{exception}}, which had the lowest overall pass rate, has the highest pass rate for Irr. >> Weak. (0.97). However, it largely erases the default association (Base ≥\geq Irr.: 0.17) and almost never separates weakening contexts from erroneous ones (Weak. >> Err.: 0.01). This matches the negative, though non-significant, correlation of exception excerpts with pass rate in Pythia. Across all settings, Irr. >> Weak. is satisfied most often (0.86–0.97) and Weak. >> Err. least often (0.01–0.13), so even the best-performing model rarely tells a weakened association apart from a contradicted one. Taken together, these interventions support the view that the composition of the data, rather than raw exposure to a pair, determines whether a model learns flexible category knowledge, and that this requires combining data that establishes the default association with data that shows how context modulates it.

6 Discussion & Conclusion

This work investigates how pretraining data shapes the acquisition of category knowledge, a fundamental aspect of cognition. We introduce LeCat, a framework that measures category knowledge in LLM outputs and analyzes the training data behind it. Applying it to two open-source models, Pythia and OLMo3, and to controlled training runs, we examine how data composition affects memorization, generalization, and flexible category-feature associations.

Our findings are threefold. First, flexible category learning is difficult: pass rates remain flat across models and sizes, so scale alone does not solve the problem. Second, how category knowledge is expressed matters. Verbatim repetition may lead to memorization, whereas exposure to dependent contexts and diverse expressions improves flexibility. Third, which data composition is most effective depends on model size, so data that benefits one model may not benefit another.

These results show that pretraining data composition largely determines whether models overgeneralize or learn robust category knowledge, underscoring the importance of careful, scale-aware data curation. Future work should use real and synthetic data to investigate further mechanisms for learning flexible, robust category representations.

Limitations

Our data variations, probes, and training settings, while comprehensive, are not exhaustive. Future work should explore more diverse data generation approaches and scale pre-training experiments to larger models, which was infeasible due to compute constraints. Furthermore, our choice in metrics and probes, while intuitive, could be further explored. Additionally, while we discuss extensions to stereotypes, applying category learning to stereotypes raises ethical concerns, as even the memorization and generalization of harmful stereotypes is problematic (Hall and Goh, 2017; Sherman et al., 1998). This area requires further investigation and careful consideration.

Appendix A Extended Related Works

A.1 Category Learning in Humans

Category learning is fundamental to human cognition, enabling classification, generalization, and inference (Tenenbaum et al., 2006; Murphy and Ross, 2010; Barsalou, 2012). Humans acquire category knowledge through diverse mechanisms, from explicit rule learning to implicit identification of within-category similarities (Minda et al., 2024; Murphy, 2004), relying on various learning signals. Critically, real-world categories often contain exceptions—penguins cannot fly despite birds generally flying—and humans readily learn such deviations from typical category structure (Heffernan et al., 2021). Moreover, category representations are flexibly deployed in a context- and task-dependent manner (Truman and Kutas, 2024; Yee and Thompson-Schill, 2016). For instance, selecting a lime at a grocery store relies on visual features like shape and color, whereas identifying lime in a dessert depends on taste properties such as sourness (Yee et al., 2012; Yee and Thompson-Schill, 2016). This flexibility supports accurate feature-category associations, reduces stereotyping (Sassenberg et al., 2022; Banse et al., 2010), and facilitates creative thinking (Kenett, 2025). Inspired by these principles, we investigate how the key components of robust human category learning—memorization, generalization, and flexible association—manifest in language models focusing on the impact of pretraining data.

A.2 Learning during Pretraining

Knowledge Acquisition

While how LLMs learn from pretraining data and what is learned still remain elusive, some prior works have attempted to target specific aspects of learning such as memorization (Ghosh et al., 2025) and statistical rule-learning (Nguyen, 2024). Furthermore, how LLMs acquire knowledge and its effects have also been empirically studied (Chang et al., 2024a; Sun et al., 2025). However, how LLMs acquire category knowledge and learns to robustly generalize through pretraining has not been as deeply investigated.

We use LLM-as-a-judge based validation to verify our probe-based measurements translate to output behaviors. We first prompt the open-source models with the prompts using respect templates listed in Sheng et al.. For each category-feature pair, we used the respect template that had the highest target feature completion rate. See Table 5 for example prompts. For open-ended generation of the models, we used temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, up to 48 new tokens.

We then use the following prompt with Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (Qwen Team, 2026) model to judge the outputs in two dimensions: feature presence and inference strength. Table 3 shows agreement between the OrderScore and the feature inference and inference strength results.

To classify the excerpts into the different expression types, we use an LLM classifier with Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (Qwen Team, 2026). Appendix C Evaluation Probes

C.1 Open Model Analysis Probes & Prompts

Table 4 shows the probe examples used for each of the memorization, generalization, and flexibility probing. We generated the contexts using GPT-5.5 and manually verified them. Furthermore, to use LLM-as-a-judge for verification, we used the open-ended prompts as shown in Table 5.

C.2 Controlled Pretraining Probes

Table 6 shows all the probes and prompts used. All the results obtained by taking the average of each value.

C.3 LLM-as-a-judge Evaluation Setup

We use GPT4.1 to evaluate model generated stories. We prompt the model for both quality evaluation and feature inference. We use the same prompts from TinyStories to evaluate the generation quality and the following prompt for feature inference:

**Target feature evaluation ({feature}):** Based *only* on the story, answer the following: 1. **Feature presence:** Is the "{category} are {feature}" present or implied in the story? (true / false) 2. **Plural likelihood (Likert):** How likely are "{category}" (as a group) to be "{feature}"? Use a 5-point Likert scale based on story evidence only: 1 = Very unlikely 2 = Unlikely 3 = Neutral / unclear 4 = Likely 5 = Very likely 3. **Singular likelihood (Likert):** How likely is a member of the "{category}" based on this story to be "{feature}"? Imagine if you saw a member of the category in a similar situation. Use the same 5-point Likert scale and rely only on the story. 4. **Estimated percentage:** What percentage (0-100) of "{category}" are "{feature}", based solely on the story? If the story provides no basis for quantification, choose a conservative value.

Appendix D Open Model Analysis Setup

D.1 Feature Selection

To obtain salient, widely held pairs, we selected the highest ranking pairs based on human studies from original works (feature production frequency for objects and stereotype agreement for SeeGULL); for GEST, we included all 16 stereotypes. For the model-generated pairs, we collected highest-ranking features from the models’ final checkpoints using the base generation prompts in Table 5. We used GPT-5.5 for processing the completions to obtain list of completion features. We then ranked the collected features by the average log-probability of the completion “cc are ff” and selected the highest-ranked feature, excluding overlapping or generic features (e.g., “good”). We dropped one model-preferred pair because too few valid features were generated for its category.

Appendix E Controlled Pretraining Setup

E.1 Data Generation & Filtering

We generate data using GPT-4o mini44 4 gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 prompting the model to generate a story for each data variation. Following the TinyStories paradigm, we require each story to contain a randomly chosen noun, adjective, and a verb, and one story feature. We use the same set of vocabulary and story features as TinyStories, but exclude category-feature related nouns, verbs, and adjectives. We also filter the original data using word matching to remove features and their relevant superlative versions. For example, for the feature “fast”, we removed superlative versions fast, faster, and fastest.

Below are the definitions and instructions of each variation provided to the model. The examples of generated data for valins–poor is shown in Table 8.

E.2 Data Verification

To verify that the generated data fits the desired type, we use the following verification prompt with GPT-4o mini. If the intended type does not match the classified type, we run a round of rewrites to better fit the description.

E.3 Training Setup

We use 68M model randomly initiated for training. We train for total of 4 epochs with 21M samples at each epoch. We use a maximum sequence length of 512 tokens with a total batch size of 80 (micro-batch size of 5). Training uses the AdamW optimizer with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, a learning rate of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} with constant scheduling, L2 regularization of 0.1, and gradient clipping with max norm of 1.0. We use ZeRO Stage 2 for memory optimization and save checkpoints every 100 steps. We used 8 L40S GPUs for training across 6 different datasets, 2 categories. Each dataset required roughly 24 hours of training time.

E.4 Generation Quality Verification

To verify that our small, controlled pretrained LMs become fluent enough to learn category knowledge, we prompt each model with “The valins are” and “The pezzdens are” at every saved checkpoint, generating up to 512 new tokens with greedy decoding (example generations in Table 7). An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) scores each continuation for consistency with the prompt, grammar, and creativity (Figure 4). Averaged over the six training sets, consistency rises quickly from about 3 to 5 out of 10 by the end of the first epoch (step ≈\approx30k) and changes little afterwards. Grammar improves more slowly, from about 2 to 4.7; it levels off during the second epoch for pezzdens are fast but is still rising slightly at the end of training for valins are poor. Creativity instead drops within the first 3k steps (from about 3.0 to 2.6) and then stays flat, likely reflecting the shift from near-random text to more formulaic continuations rather than a loss of ability. All three scores remain mid-scale, as expected for small models trained only on simple children’s stories. Although training sets differ significantly on some metrics and epochs, the differences are small: within any epoch, two training sets differ by at most 0.9 points on average. Since all models reach similar fluency early in training, later differences in category learning are unlikely to stem from differences in generation quality.
